young.html: For parents: Death in Venice is a story for adult readers. Its central theme is an older man's unhealthy obsession, and it ends in his death. Young readers can skip to the activity, and older teens may read the lesson below with a parent.

Thomas Mann was a German writer who won the Nobel Prize in 1929. This story is about a famous writer who lives by strict rules and hard work. On a holiday in Venice, the city on the water, he lets go of his rules completely, and it goes badly for him. Grown-up readers think about what happens when someone loses control of himself.

A city on the water. Venice is built on more than a hundred small islands, on wooden posts driven deep into the mud of a lagoon. People get around by boat and on foot over hundreds of bridges. Find Venice on a map of Italy. Then try building a tiny "Venice" in a tray of water with blocks or corks. What do you need so it doesn't sink?

full.html: Thomas Mann (1875–1955) grew up in Lübeck, Germany, in a merchant family whose decline he told in his first novel, Buddenbrooks (1901). He later wrote The Magic Mountain (1924), won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929, and left Germany in 1933 after the Nazis came to power, settling in the United States. Death in Venice appeared in 1912. The English translation quoted here, by Kenneth Burke, was published in 1924.
Gustav von Aschenbach is a celebrated writer in Munich, honored for books of noble self-command. He has built his life on duty and work:

full.text: Since he must carry the responsibilities of his talent on frail shoulders, and wanted to go a long way, the primary requirement was discipline—and fortunately discipline was his direct inheritance from his father's side.
full.author: Mann

full.html: Tired and restless, he sees a strange traveler at a cemetery and feels a sudden longing to go south. He ends up in Venice:

full.text: And as he looked on he thought that to reach Venice by land, on the rail-road, was like entering a palace from the rear, and that the most unreal of cities should not be approached except as he was now doing, by ship, over the high seas.
full.author: Mann

full.html: At his beach hotel he becomes fixated on a beautiful boy from a Polish family, whom he never speaks to. Meanwhile a cholera epidemic is spreading through the city, and the authorities hide it to protect the tourist trade. Aschenbach learns the truth and could warn the family or leave, but he does neither. He loses his dignity, falls ill, and dies in a beach chair. The story treats his obsession as the collapse of a life built only on willpower.

full.html: Mann sets two forces against each other: the cool discipline that made Aschenbach great, and a longing for beauty and release that he has denied all his life. When the denied side breaks through, it destroys him. Mann drew on Nietzsche's contrast of the "Apollonian" (order) and the "Dionysian" (frenzy).
The plague matters. A city that hides its sickness to protect business mirrors a man who hides the truth from himself.
Reading the story as an adventure or a romance. It is a tragedy of self-deception, told with irony by a narrator who sees more than Aschenbach does.

items: Nietzsche, earlier on this ladder, gave Mann the contrast between order and frenzy in art and life.
Plato's Phaedrus, which Aschenbach recalls in the story, discusses how beauty can lead the soul upward or astray.
Greek tragedy showed great men brought down by a flaw they would not see; Mann writes a modern version.
The story inspired an opera by Benjamin Britten (1973).
Can discipline alone make a good life? What else does a person need?
Why does Aschenbach stay in Venice when he knows about the plague?
When do communities hide bad news, and what does it cost them?
How does a writer show a character's self-deception without saying it?

questions: Aschenbach built his life on discipline. What good did it do him, and what did it leave out?
Why do you think the city hid the sickness? Was that ever right?
What should Aschenbach have done when he learned the truth?
How can rest and enjoyment be healthy, and when do they go too far?
Mann wrote with a narrator who sees more than the hero. Why might that help readers judge the hero?
care: For adult readers. The story's central theme is an older man's unhealthy obsession with a boy he never speaks to, and it ends with his death in an epidemic. The lesson summarizes at a general level, without detail.
